question: During a pre-trip inspection of the wheels and rims, what does rust around the wheel nuts most likely indicate?
choice_a: The rim has been repaired by welding
choice_b: The tire pressure is too high
choice_c: The wheel has recently been washed
choice_d: The nuts may be loose and their tightness should be checked
explanation: The manual states that rust around wheel nuts may mean the nuts are loose and instructs the driver to check tightness.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-1

question: Per the guidance on suspension system defects, what happens if one-fourth or more of the leaves in a leaf spring are missing?
choice_a: The vehicle may still be driven but must be repaired within 30 days
choice_b: It only matters if the vehicle is fully loaded
choice_c: The vehicle is placed "out of service"
choice_d: Only the axle needs replacing before the next trip
explanation: The manual specifies that missing or broken leaves in a leaf spring are dangerous, and if one-fourth or more are missing, it will put the vehicle "out of service."
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-1

question: What amount of steering wheel play is identified as being able to make a vehicle hard to steer?
choice_a: More than 45 degrees
choice_b: More than a full turn of the wheel
choice_c: Any play at all, even less than 1 degree
choice_d: More than 10 degrees (about 2 inches of movement at the rim of a 20-inch wheel)
explanation: The manual states that steering wheel play of more than 10 degrees, approximately 2 inches of movement at the rim of a 20-inch steering wheel, can make it hard to steer.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-1

question: Which combination of warning devices for a parked commercial vehicle is listed as acceptable emergency equipment?
choice_a: Three reflective triangles, or at least 6 fusees, or 3 liquid burning flares
choice_b: Four orange safety cones
choice_c: Two reflective triangles and a flashlight
choice_d: A single fusee and a spare tire
explanation: The manual lists warning devices for parked vehicles as three reflective triangles, at least 6 fusees, or 3 liquid burning flares.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-1

question: Under Step 1 of the seven-step vehicle inspection method (Vehicle Overview), what must be reviewed and what must the motor carrier do with it?
choice_a: The insurance card must be reviewed, and the carrier must update coverage
choice_b: The driver's logbook must be reviewed, and hours must be recalculated
choice_c: The last vehicle inspection report must be reviewed, and the motor carrier must repair any items affecting safety
choice_d: The vehicle registration must be reviewed, and the carrier must renew it if expired
explanation: Step 1 requires reviewing the last vehicle inspection report; the motor carrier must repair any items in the report that affect safety and certify that repairs were made or unnecessary.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-2

question: At the end of Step 4 (Turn Off Engine and Check Lights), what should a driver do before beginning the Step 5 walk-around inspection?
choice_a: Sound the horn three times
choice_b: Turn on the low-beam headlights and four-way emergency flashers before getting out of the vehicle
choice_c: Turn on the high-beam headlights only
choice_d: Leave all lights off until the walk-around is complete
explanation: Step 4 instructs the driver to set the parking brake, turn off the engine, take the key, then turn on headlights (low beams) and four-way emergency flashers before getting out of the vehicle.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-4

question: According to the gauge checks performed after starting the engine, how quickly should oil pressure come up to normal?
choice_a: Within 3 minutes
choice_b: It should stay at zero until the vehicle is in motion
choice_c: Within seconds after the engine is started
choice_d: Within 10 minutes
explanation: The manual states that oil pressure should come up to normal within seconds after the engine is started.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-3

question: When checking gauges after starting the engine, within how many minutes should air pressure build from 50 to 90 psi?
choice_a: 10 minutes
choice_b: 3 minutes
choice_c: 30 seconds
choice_d: 1 minute
explanation: The manual states air pressure should build from 50 to 90 psi within 3 minutes, then continue to governor cut-out (usually around 120-140 psi).
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-3

question: During the right-rear portion of the walk-around inspection, what should be checked regarding the wheel bearing/seals?
choice_a: Whether they are leaking
choice_b: Whether they are painted the correct color
choice_c: Whether they match the front axle bearings
choice_d: Whether they were manufactured in the current year
explanation: The walk-around inspection guide lists checking that the wheel bearing/seals are not leaking.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-5

question: Drivers of trucks and truck tractors transporting cargo must inspect the securement of the cargo within the first how many miles of a trip, and how often after that?
choice_a: Only once, at the start of the trip
choice_b: Within the first 100 miles, and every 500 miles
choice_c: Within the first 50 miles, and every 150 miles or every three hours, whichever comes first
choice_d: Within the first 10 miles, and every 50 miles
explanation: The manual requires cargo securement inspection within the first 50 miles of a trip and every 150 miles or every three hours after, whichever comes first.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-6

question: When performing the Step 7 check for hydraulic brake leaks, what should a driver do?
choice_a: Apply the parking brake and rev the engine to 2000 rpm
choice_b: Pump the brake pedal ten times rapidly
choice_c: Pump the brake pedal three times, then apply firm pressure and hold it for five seconds, checking that the pedal does not move
choice_d: Release the brake pedal and coast for 100 feet
explanation: The manual instructs pumping the brake pedal three times, then applying firm pressure and holding for five seconds; if the pedal moves, there may be a leak.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-6

question: For a manual-transmission commercial vehicle, what should a driver do to avoid rolling back when starting?
choice_a: Fully release the clutch before pressing the accelerator
choice_b: Shift directly into second gear
choice_c: Partly engage the clutch before taking the right foot off the brake
choice_d: Always rely on the trailer brake hand valve, even on vehicles without one
explanation: The manual advises that with a manual transmission, the driver should partly engage the clutch before taking the right foot off the brake to avoid rolling back.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-7

question: What is the recommended way to hold the steering wheel while driving a commercial vehicle?
choice_a: With one hand resting on the gearshift
choice_b: Firmly, with both hands on opposite sides of the wheel
choice_c: Loosely, to allow the wheel to self-correct
choice_d: With both hands at the top of the wheel only
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to hold the steering wheel firmly with both hands on opposite sides, so the wheel does not pull away from their hands if they hit a curb or pothole.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-7

question: When stopping a commercial vehicle, how should a driver apply the brake pedal for a smooth, safe stop?
choice_a: Apply the parking brake instead of the foot brake
choice_b: Push the brake pedal down gradually and control the pressure
choice_c: Push the brake pedal down as hard as possible immediately
choice_d: Pump the brake pedal rapidly at all times
explanation: The manual states to push the brake pedal down gradually and control the pressure so the vehicle comes to a smooth, safe stop.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-7

question: Why does the manual recommend backing and turning toward the driver's side whenever possible?
choice_a: Because the right side mirror is typically unavailable
choice_b: Because it reduces fuel consumption
choice_c: Because the driver can see better by looking out the side window, unlike when backing toward the right side
choice_d: Because it is required by federal law in all circumstances
explanation: The manual explains that backing to the driver's side lets the driver watch the rear of the vehicle through the side window, while backing toward the right side is very dangerous because visibility is worse.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-7

question: What backing technique does the manual recommend to make it easier to correct steering errors and stop quickly if necessary?
choice_a: Back only while watching the rearview mirror, never out the window
choice_b: Back at normal driving speed to avoid stalling
choice_c: Back as slowly as possible, using the lowest reverse gear
choice_d: Back using the highest reverse gear available
explanation: The manual's backing safety rules include backing as slowly as possible and using the lowest reverse gear so steering errors can be corrected and the vehicle stopped quickly.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-7

question: Which type of manual transmission requires double clutching to change gears, according to the manual?
choice_a: All automatic transmissions
choice_b: None -- double clutching is never required
choice_c: Unsynchronized manual transmissions
choice_d: Synchronized manual transmissions
explanation: The manual states that most heavy vehicles with unsynchronized manual transmissions require double clutching, while double clutching is NOT required on a synchronized manual transmission.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-8

question: Why does the manual recommend downshifting to a low gear before starting down a hill?
choice_a: So the vehicle can be controlled without using the brakes hard, preventing them from overheating and losing braking power
choice_b: So the parking brake can be engaged for the entire descent
choice_c: So the engine can be turned off while coasting downhill
choice_d: So the driver can safely shift into neutral
explanation: The manual explains that downshifting before starting down a hill lets you control speed without using the brakes hard, since overheated brakes can lose their braking power.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-8

question: How many basic types of retarders does the manual describe, and when should a retarder be turned off?
choice_a: Six types; retarders should never be turned off once activated
choice_b: Two types (electric and hydraulic); turn it off only in dry conditions
choice_c: Three types (engine, exhaust, and mechanical); turn it off only above 55 mph
choice_d: Four types (exhaust, engine, hydraulic, and electric); turn it off when the road is wet, icy, or snow covered
explanation: The manual lists four basic types of retarders (exhaust, engine, hydraulic, electric) and cautions that the retarder should be turned off whenever the road is wet, icy, or snow covered because it may cause drive wheels to skid.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-9

question: According to the manual, how far ahead should most good drivers look while driving?
choice_a: At least 12 to 15 seconds ahead
choice_b: About 2 to 3 seconds ahead
choice_c: Only as far as the vehicle's headlights reach
choice_d: At least one full minute ahead
explanation: The manual states that most good drivers look at least 12 to 15 seconds ahead, which is about one block at lower speeds or about a quarter mile at highway speeds.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-10

question: When can mirror adjustment be checked accurately, according to the manual?
choice_a: Only while the vehicle is parked on a hill
choice_b: Only while the vehicle is in reverse
choice_c: Only after the engine has been running for 30 minutes
choice_d: When the trailer(s) are straight
explanation: The manual states that mirror adjustment should be checked prior to the start of any trip and can only be checked accurately when the trailer(s) are straight.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-10

question: What visual effect do curved (convex) mirrors have on the appearance of objects, according to the manual?
choice_a: Objects appear upside down
choice_b: Objects appear larger and closer than they really are
choice_c: Objects appear smaller and farther away than they really are
choice_d: Objects appear exactly the same size as in a flat mirror
explanation: The manual explains that everything appears smaller in a convex mirror than it would look directly, and things also seem farther away than they really are.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-10

question: Per the manual's guidance on checking mirrors during a lane change, what should a driver check right after signaling?
choice_a: That no one has moved into the driver's blind spot
choice_b: That the fuel gauge reads full
choice_c: That the trailer brake hand valve is engaged
choice_d: That the parking brake is released
explanation: The manual lists checking mirrors after you have signaled to make sure no one has moved into your blind spot, as part of the lane-change mirror-check sequence.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-10

question: What three rules does the manual give for using turn signals?
choice_a: Signal only for right turns, signal loudly with the horn, and cancel before turning
choice_b: Signal only when another vehicle is nearby, signal briefly, and leave the signal on afterward
choice_c: Signal after beginning the turn, signal intermittently, and leave it on until the next turn
choice_d: Signal early, signal continuously, and cancel the signal after completing the turn
explanation: The manual gives three rules for turn signals: signal early, signal continuously (don't cancel until the turn is complete), and cancel the signal after turning.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-11

question: When about to pass a vehicle, pedestrian, or bicyclist who may not see you, what does the manual recommend doing when it is legal?
choice_a: Tap the horn lightly, or at night, flash your lights from low to high beam and back
choice_b: Flash your hazard lights continuously until you have passed
choice_c: Honk the horn continuously until the pass is complete
choice_d: Immediately swerve into the next lane without warning
explanation: The manual advises tapping the horn lightly, or at night flashing lights from low to high beam and back, when passing someone who may not see you, while still driving carefully in case they don't respond.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-11

question: On a two-lane road carrying traffic in both directions, where should warning devices be placed to mark a stopped vehicle's location?
choice_a: Within 10 feet of the front or rear corners, and 100 feet behind and ahead of the vehicle
choice_b: 500 feet behind and 500 feet ahead of the vehicle only
choice_c: 50 feet behind and 200 feet ahead of the vehicle
choice_d: Only directly behind the vehicle, no more than 10 feet away
explanation: The manual states that on a two-lane road carrying traffic in both directions, warning devices should be placed within 10 feet of the front or rear corners to mark the vehicle's location, plus 100 feet behind and ahead of it.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-12

question: What is the average perception time for an alert driver, and how far does a vehicle travel during that time at 55 mph, according to the manual?
choice_a: About 5 seconds, accounting for 400 feet traveled
choice_b: About 3 seconds, accounting for 250 feet traveled
choice_c: About 1/2 second, accounting for 20 feet traveled
choice_d: About 1-3/4 seconds, accounting for 142 feet traveled
explanation: The manual states the average perception time for an alert driver is 1-3/4 seconds, which at 55 mph accounts for 142 feet traveled.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-13

question: According to the manual, if you double your speed from 20 to 40 mph, how much greater is the impact and braking distance?
choice_a: 16 times greater
choice_b: 8 times greater
choice_c: 4 times greater
choice_d: 2 times greater
explanation: The manual states that doubling speed from 20 to 40 mph makes the impact 4 times greater, and the braking distance is also 4 times longer.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-13

question: At what speed does the manual say hydroplaning can occur if there is a lot of water on the road?
choice_a: Hydroplaning cannot occur below highway speeds
choice_b: As low as 30 mph
choice_c: Only above 55 mph
choice_d: Only above 70 mph
explanation: The manual states that hydroplaning can occur at speeds as low as 30 mph if there is a lot of water, and is more likely with low tire pressure or worn tread.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-14

question: On a wet road, approximately how much should a driver reduce speed, according to the manual's example?
choice_a: By about two-thirds (e.g., slow from 55 to about 18 mph)
choice_b: No reduction is needed if the vehicle has good tires
choice_c: By about one-third (e.g., slow from 55 to about 35 mph)
choice_d: By about one-tenth (e.g., slow from 55 to about 50 mph)
explanation: The manual instructs reducing speed by about one-third on a wet road, giving the example of slowing from 55 to about 35 mph.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-14
